files.lesson.md: --- order: 22 unit: quad9 node: AC9M9A05 n1 uses: [AC9M9A04 n1] assumes: [AC9M9A04 n1] connection: stopping-distance title: Linear or quadratic? summary: "A straight line has equal first differences and a quadratic has equal second differences. Real data fits neither exactly, so you pick the better model and say why." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Why does 60 km/h take so much longer to stop than 50 km/h, when it is only 10 km/h faster?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8369 url: http://127.0.0.1:8369/index.html readySelector: "#board" layout: full --- Real measurements are never perfectly straight or perfectly curved. Choosing a model means asking which pattern fits better, and where it stops working. ## Predict: stopping at 60 ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to a stopping distance at 60 km/h from the pattern in the first three speeds shows who keeps adding the same amount and who allows the amount to grow." check: type: predict q: "Transport for NSW gives typical stopping distances on a reasonable road: about 19 m at 30 km/h, 27 m at 40 km/h and 37 m at 50 km/h. Following the pattern, what is the stopping distance at 60 km/h?" options: - "46 m" - "47 m" - "49 m" - "56 m" actual: "About 56 m, the published figure. A steady 9 m more for each 10 km/h would give 46 m. Even the extra growing by 2 each time would give 49 m. The real distance grows faster than both." ``` The figures are from the [Transport for NSW speeding page](https://www.transport.nsw.gov.au/roadsafety/topics-tips/speeding), checked 25 October 2026. They are typical values on a reasonable road surface: the surface, the tyres and the driver all change them. The bars are drawn to scale for the first three speeds. How tall is the last one? ## Run: fit a line ```step stage: run insight: "A line that fits the first three points exactly falls short at the fourth: the real data is curving upward away from the line." try: { playground: board, starter: "stop.yml#run", height: 560 } check: { type: board, text: "Set $m$ and $c$ so the line goes through the first three points. Where does the fourth point sit? Was your prediction right?", when: "m = 9 and c = -8" } ``` On the board, $x$ is the speed in tens of km/h ($x = 3$ is 30 km/h) and $y$ is the stopping distance in metres. The dots are the published figures. ## Investigate: differences ```step stage: investigate insight: "Equal first differences mean a line, equal second differences a quadratic. The real distances (19, 27, 37, 56) have first differences 8, 10, 19, which aren't equal, and second differences 2 and 9, which aren't equal either, so neither is exact." tasks: - check: type: number q: "The stopping distances at 30, 40, 50 and 60 km/h are $19, 27, 37, 56$ m. What is the first difference between 50 and 60 km/h?" answer: 19 explain: "56 − 37 = 19 m." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "What is $56 - 37$?", answer: 19, explain: "56 − 37 = 19." } - check: type: question q: "The first differences are $8, 10, 19$. What does that say about a straight-line model?" options: ["A line doesn't fit: the distance goes up by more for each extra 10 km/h", "A line fits well: the distance always goes up", "A line fits exactly: the differences are all even or odd", "You can't tell from three differences"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Going up isn't enough: a line goes up by the same amount each time.", "The differences are 8, 10, 19: not equal, and parity doesn't matter.", "Three differences are enough to see they aren't equal."] explain: "A line needs equal first differences. These grow, so the data curves upward." - check: type: question q: "The distance a car travels while the driver reacts grows in step with speed. The braking distance grows with the square of the speed. What shape is the total stopping distance?" options: ["Curved upward: a mix of a straight part and a squared part", "A straight line", "A curve that bends downward", "A flat line"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The squared part makes it curve.", "A squared term curves upward, not downward.", "The distance changes with speed."] explain: "Reaction distance is linear and braking distance is quadratic, so the total curves upward." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#pat" text: "Pat estimates the distance at 60 km/h from the first two figures. Click the line where his working goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: assume-linear-from-one-step explain: "Line 3: one step doesn't set the pattern. The next differences are 10 and 19, not 8, so the estimate of 43 m is far too low." ``` ### The jump to 60 To choose a model, look at the differences. Equal first differences mean a line. Equal second differences mean a quadratic. ```worked \text{Table A: } 2, 5, 8, 11 :: Four values at equal steps. \text{first differences: } 3, 3, 3 :: Equal, so linear. \text{Table B: } 1, 4, 9, 16 :: Another table. \text{first differences: } 3, 5, 7 :: Not equal. \text{second differences: } 2, 2 :: Equal, so quadratic. \text{real data } 19, 27, 37, 56 :: Neither is exactly equal. \text{choose the better model and say why} :: And say where it stops working. ``` Work out the differences of $19, 27, 37, 56$ on paper, then answer. ### A straight line? ### Why it curves ### Find the mistake Read Pat's working. Which line assumes the pattern? ## Modify: change the speed ```step stage: modify insight: "Using the figures for new speeds shows that the gap grows and that a model has limits: it can give an impossible answer outside the data." tasks: - hint: ["Use the published figures for 50 and 60 km/h.", "56 − 37."] check: { type: number, q: "A council cuts a speed limit from 60 to 50 km/h. How many metres shorter is the typical stopping distance?", answer: 19, explain: "56 − 37 = 19 m. A 10 km/h cut saves a lot more at the high end." } - hint: ["A line through the last two points goes up 19 per 10 km/h.", "The data is curving upward."] check: { type: question, q: "A line through the last two points (50 and 60 km/h) predicts 75 m at 70 km/h. Is that likely to be a safe estimate?", options: ["No: the real distance probably grows faster, so it would be an underestimate", "Yes: a line is always safe", "Yes: the data is already linear", "No: it's an overestimate"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "The data curves upward, so a line falls short further out.", "The first differences keep growing.", "The data is curving upward, so the line falls below it."], explain: "The first differences have been growing, so the next one is likely bigger than 19. The line would underestimate." } - hint: ["At 0 km/h the car is already stopped.", "What does the line y = 9x − 8 give at x = 0?"] check: { type: question, q: "Edge case: the line $y = 9x - 8$ gives $-8$ at $x = 0$ (0 km/h). What does that tell you?", options: ["The line isn't a good model near 0: a stopped car needs 0 m", "A stopped car needs −8 m to stop", "The line is exact", "The speed can be negative"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "A distance can't be negative.", "An impossible answer shows the model has limits.", "Speed isn't negative here."], explain: "A model fitted to speeds from 30 to 60 km/h is only reliable in that range." } ``` ### Cutting the limit ### Going further ### Zero speed ## Practise: choose the model ```step stage: practise insight: "Using first and second differences to decide, and saying when neither fits exactly." tasks: - check: type: number q: "A table gives $y = 2, 5, 10, 17$ for $x = 1, 2, 3, 4$. What is the second difference?" answer: 2 explain: "First differences 3, 5, 7. Second differences 2, 2." - check: type: question q: "A table gives $y = 4, 9, 14, 19$. Which model fits?" options: ["Linear: the first differences are all 5", "Quadratic: the second differences are 5", "Neither", "Exponential"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The first differences are equal, so a line fits.", "A line fits exactly.", "The values go up by the same amount, not the same factor."] explain: "9 − 4 = 5, 14 − 9 = 5, 19 − 14 = 5: equal first differences." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "What is $9 - 4$?", answer: 5, explain: "9 − 4 = 5." } - check: type: question q: "A table gives $y = 3, 4, 7, 13$ for $x = 1, 2, 3, 4$. Which is the best description?" options: ["Curving upward: neither exact, but a curve fits better than a line", "A perfect line", "A perfect quadratic", "No pattern at all"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The first differences are 1, 3, 6: not equal.", "The second differences are 2 and 3: not equal.", "The values grow faster and faster: a curve describes that better than a line."] explain: "First differences 1, 3, 6 and second differences 2, 3: not exact, but clearly curving upward." - check: type: number q: "Review: solve $x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0$. What is the larger solution?" answer: 4 explain: "(x − 1)(x − 4) = 0, so x = 1 or x = 4." ``` ### Second difference ### A line? ### Neither exact ### Review From the last unit: solving by factorising. ## Make: the speed limit ```step stage: make insight: "Returning to the stopping distances: measure how far a straight-line model is out and say why that matters for a speed limit." tasks: - hint: ["The line y = 9x − 8 at x = 6 is 46.", "The published figure is 56."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A line through the first three figures predicts 46 m at 60 km/h. The published figure is 56 m. By how many metres does the line under-estimate?" steps: - ["$9 \\times 6 - 8 = 46$", "what the line says at x = 6"] - ["$56 - 46 = 10$", "the real figure minus the line"] - ["10 m", "the line under-estimates by 10 m"] answer: "10" answerLabel: "Under-estimate (m)" tolerance: 0.001 feedback: - ["46", "That's the line's prediction. Subtract it from 56."] - ["56", "That's the real figure. Find how far the line misses it."] criteria: - "I worked out what the line says before comparing." - "I subtracted in the right order (real minus line)." - "I gave the answer in metres." explain: "56 − 46 = 10 m. The line is 10 m short at 60 km/h." - check: type: question q: "Why does this matter for choosing a speed limit?" options: ["A line would under-estimate how far cars need to stop at higher speeds", "A line would over-estimate how far cars need to stop", "The model makes no difference", "Faster cars always stop sooner"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The line falls below the real figure at 60 km/h.", "The gap is 10 m at 60 km/h.", "Using a model that's too low could put a stop line or a crossing in the wrong place."] explain: "At higher speeds, the real distance is more than the line says, so a line would make roads look safer than they are." ``` ### How far out? Back to the stopping distances. Work it out on paper first, then type your answer. ### Why it matters The stopping distances are typical values on a reasonable road surface from [Transport for NSW](https://www.transport.nsw.gov.au/roadsafety/topics-tips/speeding). Real distances depend on the road, tyres and driver. **Also used in** - **Road safety.** Speed limits near schools and crossings are set knowing that stopping distance grows faster than speed. - **Science.** Many real measurements are almost a straight line over a short range and curve outside it. - **Next lesson.** Using the model to answer a question and saying where the answer stops being reliable. ```teacher summary: Students use first and second differences to compare a straight-line and a quadratic model of real stopping distances, and say where each fails (AC9M9A05, node 1). time: 40 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 12 min goals: - I can use differences to decide between a line and a curve. - I can say when neither model fits exactly. - I can say why an under-estimate matters in a real situation. struggle: "Expecting a perfect pattern. Ask: do the differences have to match exactly for the model to be useful?" before: > Students need Recognising a quadratic. The one idea: choose the model whose pattern is closer, and say how far it is out and where it stops working. The common mistake is assuming a rate from one step (Pat's working). The figures are typical stopping distances from Transport for NSW (checked 25 October 2026) on a reasonable road surface. They don't separate reaction and braking distances, so the lesson says that split from the physics, not from the table. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Those who chose 46 or 47 kept the rate steady. Reveal the real figure after Run." - "Run: ask students to say, before setting m and c, how much each 10 km/h should add." - "Paper: the try-one after the worked example and the under-estimate in Make are worked on paper first. Books out, and look for the differences written out." - "Modify: before the zero-speed question, ask what a stopped car needs." stuck: - see: A student says the data is linear because it always goes up. ask: Are the differences equal? fix: "8, 10, 19: no. A line needs equal differences." - see: A student says the data must be quadratic because it curves. ask: Are the second differences equal? fix: "2 and 9: not exactly. It's a better fit than a line, but not exact." stretch: Fit y = ax² + bx to the points at 30 and 60 km/h, and see how far it is out at 40 and 50. support: A printed table with space for both rows of differences. leads: > Continues AC9M9A05 node 1. Where it leads: Solving the model and saying what the answer means, then reporting its limits. exit: q: A table has first differences 4, 4, 4. Linear, quadratic or neither? a: "Linear: the first differences are equal." explain: > A line has equal first differences. A quadratic has equal second differences. Real data usually fits neither exactly. Choose the better model, say how far it is out, and say where it stops working. ```

# Boards for "Linear or quadratic?". Transport for NSW typical stopping distances; x is speed in tens of km/h.

# region: run
widget: graph
x: 0, 8
y: -10, 70
grid: 1, 10
axes: Speed (tens of km/h), Distance (m)
slider m: 0, 15, 4, 1
slider c: -20, 20, 0, 1
series Data: 3,19; 4,27; 5,37; 6,56
plot: y = mx + c
# endregion
files.working.txt:
# Pat's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: pat
Stopping distance: 19 m at 30 km/h, 27 m at 40 km/h.
From 30 to 40 km/h the distance goes up by 8 m.
So every 10 km/h more adds 8 m.
At 60 km/h: 19 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 43 m.
# endregion
